opener.heading: Week 47: Seasons & Nature Cycles 🍂
about: Everything she counts this week came off a tree, out of the ground or in from the garden. Potatoes into four bowls on Friday, six scoops into six jars on Sunday, twenty-nine pebbles into a countdown jar on Monday. The number work sits inside the season, and the season keeps handing her things worth counting. By Tuesday the whole year is a paper circle she can spin from December round to January again, and the jar that started on Monday runs on past this week to the night she turns four. Wednesday puts a board on a stack of books and lets her make the hill steeper herself.

Thanksgiving lands on Thursday and takes the day. She makes one dish for the table with nobody else's hands in it, lumps and all, then walks the block naming one thank-you at every corner. The afternoon gives her the far corner of the living room and a car built from dining chairs, which keeps both children busy and out of a hot kitchen while the house fills up.
azlyn: One-to-one counting. One number word for one object, with her hand moving each thing as she says it, and small groups landing whole before any counting starts.
A unit has to hold its size. Six scoops means something while the scoop stays the same, and the swap to a mug shows her why.
Counting down. Twenty-nine to one, one pebble a night, a smaller number said out loud each time.
The year comes round. Twelve months with faces on them, four seasons in four quarters, December turning back into January.
She can change the slope. One more book under the end and everything runs further, and her hands put the book there.
you: Touching each thing as she counts is what stops her double-counting
Recognizing three without counting has a name, and it arrives before counting does
A unit only works if it stays the same size, and that's the hard part
Counting down is much harder than counting up
Giving a number a personality is what makes it stick
Steeper is a variable she can control, and that's rare
Driving somewhere imaginary requires her to hold a destination in mind
shopping: Potatoes, 6 for Thursday plus whatever comes in on Friday
Apples and onions, however many you have
Rice and lentils, 2 bags of each; oats, 1 bag
Butter, milk and salt, for Thursday's mash
Jars with lids, 14: 6 for Friday, 6 clear ones for Sunday, 2 for Monday
1 large tub, wide enough for her to mix in with both arms
1 yogurt pot, 1 egg cup, 1 large mug and 1 spoon, for the scoops
1 potato masher, 1 wooden spoon and 1 serving dish
Paper plates, 10, or circles cut from card
Thick card, 16 postcard-sized pieces: 10 for Saturday, the rest for Tuesday's name cards
Paper, a stack, for labels, records, her map and a rolled funnel
1 long strip of paper: a wallpaper offcut, or 4 sheets taped end to end
Cardboard, 1 piece big enough for a steering wheel circle
Sticky tape, and masking tape if you have it
White school glue, or double-sided tape
Envelopes, 15: 12 for the door, 3 for Kreston
1 brass fastener, for the wheel, if you skip the wool
1 flat board, an ironing board, or a big flattened box
Books of the same thickness, a stack of 8–10
1 log slice from the firewood pile, or a photo of a cut stump
1 bag, with a snack and a drink in it for the car
1 low shelf, or a shallow box
Photos of everyone in the family, and one of the tree in summer
1 pressed leaf, if you kept one
Thick card, 1 sheet, for November's handprint
A wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 17 months this week. He kicks a ball with his whole leg and misses about half the time, and two-word combinations are starting, so listen for more jar and big tree.

days.title: The Harvest Count
days.prepTonight: Pile everything from the yard and the market onto the kitchen table, get four big bowls down, and wash six jars for the afternoon.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Bringing In the Last of It

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Four Bowls and Everything That Came In

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Shelf That Has to Get Us to Spring

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, Then the Book About the Seasons

opening.title: Bringing In the Last of It
opening.need: the pile of vegetables, fruit and nuts · 1 squash · 4 large bowls.
steps: Sit her at the table with the whole pile in front of her and no instruction for a minute.
Set the four bowls out and name them: potatoes, apples, onions, nuts. She moves things across, and the squash stays in the middle.
Ask which bowl she thinks holds the most. Take her answer and tell her you both find out at 9:15.

main.title: Four Bowls and Everything That Came In
materials: Potatoes, apples and onions, however many came in
1 bag of nuts in their shells
Chalk, or paper and a marker
steps: Empty the four bowls back onto the table. Potatoes first: she lifts one, you wipe it with the dish towel, she says the number, and it goes into the bowl.
Chalk the total beside the bowl. Do the apples the same way, then the onions.
When she skips a number, say nothing and start that bowl again from one.
Nuts next, the hard bowl: all one color, all one size. Lay them in a long line and let her walk a finger along the row.
Tip out the dried beans and ask her to count those too. Let her go as long as she wants, then chalk TOO MANY beside the bag.
Last, the squash. One. Chalk a big 1, then cut it open yourself with her standing back and let her scoop the seeds onto the table. One outside, too many inside.
main.tip: She will point at the same potato twice. Moving each one into the bowl as she names it keeps the counted pile and the waiting pile apart.

outside.title: What's Left on the Branches
paras: Walk the usual route and hunt for anything still hanging on. Rosehips, hawthorn berries, a few crab apples, the odd apple nobody could reach. Count what you find on each tree and say the number out loud underneath it. Bare branches make the loaded ones stand out from the end of the street.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and copies whatever job is going. Put a small bowl of his own on the high-chair tray with three potatoes beside it, and let him load them in and tip them out again while the counting runs. On the walk he manages a good stretch on his own feet if you stop at every gate.

second.title: The Shelf That Has to Get Us to Spring
second.intro: The branches this morning were nearly empty. The counted food goes into jars on one low shelf that stays full all winter.
materials: Dried beans, rice, lentils and pasta
1 rolled paper cone as a funnel
1 low shelf, or a shallow box
steps: Stand the six jars along the table, lids off to one side.
Hold the paper cone in the first jar and let her pour the beans in from the bag. Rice, lentils and pasta fill the next three.
The last two jars are hers. One takes this morning's nuts. She picks what goes in the other.
She draws what is inside on a scrap of paper, one label per jar, and you write the word underneath. Tape each label to its jar.
Marker on every lid: today's date. Say the date out loud as you write it.
Clear the low shelf and let her carry the jars over one at a time. The order is hers.
Sit on the floor with her and count along the shelf. Six.
second.tip: Cook from that shelf. A jar she filled and watched you empty into a pan in February beats a row she gets told not to touch.

alternatives: Fill two jars and leave the shelf for another day.
Sort the nuts by size into an egg box.
Peel apples into rings and dry them over the radiator.
Draw round the squash on the biggest paper you own.
outAgain: The café, cake and a window seat, and count the people who come through the door
The market before it packs up, for whatever is cheap and in season
The produce market, and let her carry one bag home
Home early with the heating on, if the morning ran long

aroundWorld.title: Korea, Chuseok and Songpyeon 🌾
paras: Korean families mark Chuseok by steaming songpyeon, half-moon rice cakes filled with sesame and honey. Ga families in Ghana sprinkle kpokpoi, a corn dish, along the streets at Homowo before anyone sits down to eat. Jewish families eat for a week in a sukkah, a booth roofed with loose branches, built once the harvest is in.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Make one half-moon dumpling from any dough in the house, filled with a spoonful of honey and sesame seeds, and steam it. Azlyn crimps the edge shut with her thumb.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: A sukkah roof has to be thin enough to see stars through, or it does not count.

days.krestonPM: Give him one empty jar and its lid and let him work at getting the lid on and off. At 17 months he stays with it longer than with any toy you could buy. He can carry one closed jar to the shelf and hand it up to Azlyn. Two-word combinations are starting, so listen out for more jar or my one while he works.

insight.headline: Touching each thing as she counts is what stops her double-counting.
paras: Azlyn can recite to twenty and still tell you a row of six potatoes has nine in it. Reciting and counting are separate skills, and the second rests on one-to-one correspondence: one number word, one object, nothing missed and nothing used twice. Her hand enforces it. Researchers who watch three-year-olds count find that the ones who point or move each item make far fewer errors than the ones counting by eye. Moving each potato into a bowl as she names it puts the rule into her hands a year before she could explain it, and she drops the pointing on her own once she stops needing it.

days.safety: The knife for the squash is adult-only and goes back out of reach the moment the squash is open. Nuts in their shells, dried beans and small hard vegetables are all choking hazards for a 17-month-old who walks over and helps himself, so count with Kreston in the high chair and sweep the floor before he is down.

days.title: Three Without Counting
days.prepTonight: Cut ten postcard-sized pieces from thick card and leave them on a tray with the glue, a bag of dried beans, the sunflower seeds and a handful of small cones.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Gone Before She Can Count It

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Smell of Pine by the Door

opening.title: Grab Three, Don't Count
opening.need: a bowl of dried beans · 1 shallow tray.
steps: Tip a handful of beans onto the tray and sit down opposite her.
Ask her to grab three. One grab, no counting out loud, no pointing. She opens her hand and you both count what she got.
Run it a dozen times, asking for two, then four, then three again. She lands three more often than any other number, so say so out loud.

main.title: Gone Before She Can Count It
materials: Thick card, cut into 10 postcard-sized pieces
White school glue, or double-sided tape
steps: Lay the ten cards out on the tray and hand her the glue. Her job is a blob wherever a seed is going.
First five cards, beans: one bean, then two, then three, four, five. She counts them onto the glue herself.
Second five cards, cones and sunflower seeds, same numbers again. Set these in different shapes: three in a row on one card, three in a triangle on the next.
Write the number on the back of each card with the marker, then leave them for twenty minutes to dry.
Now the game. Hold a card up for one second, take it away, and ask how many. Stay on one, two and three to begin with.
Move up to four and five and watch the moment she starts counting instead of knowing.
main.tip: Never say count them on the low cards. One prompt from you turns the whole game into counting practice.

outside.title: The Green That Stays Green
paras: Late November has stripped everything else back, so what stays green shows up from the end of the road. Hunt for moss on a north-facing curb, pine, spruce and cedar in the front yards. Break a few stems off by hand where you have permission, three at a time, and bring them home in a bag for one o'clock.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and wants a job with a container in it. Go through the bag yourself first, then hand it to him and let him drop the stems back in. He will take them out again and hand them to Azlyn. Watch his mouth, because every leaf he picks up is heading for it.

second.title: Three Stems in Every Bundle
second.intro: The clippings come in cold and smelling of the hedge. They get tied into bundles of three, and the best bundle hangs on the front door until Christmas.
materials: The evergreen clippings from the walk: pine, spruce or cedar
1 loop of string to hang it from the door knocker
steps: Spread the clippings across the table and sort them into piles by kind. She decides what counts as the same.
Her job is bundles of three stems. No counting out loud, no pointing. Grab and check by eye.
Check each bundle as she finishes it. Any bundle of four goes back on the pile and gets made again.
Trim the bottom ends level with the scissors so each bundle sits flat. You cut, she holds the top of the bundle.
Wrap string round each bundle three times and knot it. Her finger goes on the crossover while you pull the knot tight.
Pick the best bundle between you and tie the ribbon round it in a bow.
Thread the loop of string under the binding and hang it on the door knocker.
second.tip: Let her build the ugly bundles too. Three straggly spruce ends are the same three as three good pine ones, and mixing them stops three meaning pine in her head.

alternatives: One bundle only, hung on the door, and stop there.
Stand the clippings in a pitcher of water and call it done.
Press a few spruce and cedar sprigs between two heavy books.
Sort the whole pile by smell instead of by kind.
outAgain: The botanical garden, glasshouses first while the weather does what it likes
The garden center, for the smell of the Christmas trees going in
A hedge walk to look for berries you left behind this morning
The park with the pine trees, and count the cones under one of them
A friend's house, if the bundle is done by three
days.krestonPM: Give him one soft pine stem to hold and keep the rest of the pile up on the table. At 17 months he is kicking anything ball shaped, so roll a cone across the floor to him and let him boot it back. He aims with the whole leg and misses about half the time.

insight.headline: Recognizing three without counting has a name, and it arrives before counting does.
paras: Show Azlyn two beans and she does not count them. Show her three and most of the time she still does not. Psychologists call it subitizing, and it works up to about four items before the brain hands over to counting. Babies do a version of it in their first year, long before number words exist for them. Her counting sits on top of that older ability, which is why a small group comes out instant and confident while six potatoes need a finger and a bowl. Flashing a card for one second exercises the fast system on its own, and she will use that system for the rest of her life.

days.safety: Every part of a yew is poisonous, the needles and bark as much as the berries, so leave it where it is. Holly berries are poisonous too, and Kreston mouths every leaf he can reach, so go through the bag yourself before it reaches him. Sort the pile up on the table, not down where he is. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: How Many Cupfuls
days.prepTonight: Stand the big tub on the table with the bags of beans, rice, lentils and oats beside it, and start a pile of twenty-nine flat pebbles or wine corks for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Tub and the Six Scoops

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Bag of Leaves That Waits Till Spring

opening.title: The Tub and the Six Scoops
opening.need: 1 large tub · the bags of beans, rice, lentils and oats · a yogurt pot, an egg cup and a spoon.
steps: Tip all four bags into the tub and let her mix them with both arms until she is bored.
Lay the yogurt pot, the egg cup and the spoon in front of her. Agree on the yogurt pot together, and put the other two away.
Six scoops out of the tub and six back in, counting out loud.

main.title: The Same Cup Every Time
materials: 1 large tub of mixed dried beans, rice, lentils and oats
1 yogurt pot, chosen this morning as the scoop
Paper labels, 1 marker and sticky tape
steps: Stand the tub and the empty jars on the tray. Everything happens on the tray.
Six scoops from the tub into jar one, and she says each number as the pot goes in. Lid on. She copies 6 onto a label, you stick it on.
Jars two and three the same way, same pot, same count. Stand all three in a row so she sees the levels match.
Jar four gets the mug. Six scoops again, counted the same. It overflows before she reaches six.
Ask what went wrong and give her a long silence. The number was right both times, and she picks the pot back up to show you.
Jars five and six are hers to fill with whichever tool she wants. Label them, and stand the mug's jar at the end of the row.
main.tip: Do not warn her about the mug beforehand. A heads-up from you turns the overflow into a demonstration she watched rather than a mistake she made.

outside.title: How Deep the Leaves Got
paras: Find the corner where the wind has piled the leaves deepest, against a fence or in the lee of a wall. Stand her in it and see where they come up to: over the boot, past the ankle, halfway to the knee. Do three places and name a winner. Make the last one your own yard, and tell her that pile is this afternoon's job.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and leaf piles are the best thing outdoors for him. Set him down in a clear patch and let him wade, kick and fall over in it. He will hand you single leaves for ten minutes, so take each one.

second.title: The Bag of Leaves That Waits Till Spring
second.intro: This afternoon's pile is the corner of the yard the wind fills every year. The bucket is the unit now, and the bag waits in a sheltered corner until it turns into soil.
materials: 1 bucket, used as the counting unit
Gardening gloves for both of you
Thick card, 1 sheet, for November's handprint
Washable non-toxic poster paint and 1 wide soft brush
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Gloves on, hers first, and let her do the fastening.
She fills the bucket with hands while you loosen the packed leaves with the fork. Full to the rim counts, half full does not.
Bucketful one goes into the first trash bag. Say one out loud as it tips and keep the count running. Every three bucketfuls, both of you tread it down, then carry on from where the count stopped.
Fill the second bag once the first is full, and start a fresh count at one.
Write the number of bucketfuls, the date and LEAVES on each bag while she watches. Tie the necks with string.
Drag the bags to the sheltered corner together. Tell her they open in spring and what comes out is not leaves.

Gloves off, hands washed, and the November handprint sheet comes out on the kitchen table. Kreston's palm goes first while he is calm, washcloth already in your other hand, and November and 17 months go beside his print. Azlyn's goes on the same sheet. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write November and 3 beside it.
second.tip: Punch a few holes in each bag with the fork before you tie it, and wet the leaves if they are dry. A wet bag with air in it is soil by April; a dry sealed one is still leaves.

alternatives: One bag, twenty minutes, done.
Rake into one enormous pile and jump in it instead.
Sort the best leaves by color on the doorstep.
No yard: one bag filled at the park and stood on the balcony till spring.
outAgain: A nature hunt walk, one bag and a list of five things to find
The woods, for the deepest leaf drift you can get to
The duck pond, and count the ducks still on it this late in the year
A hill with a view, for how far you can see now the trees are bare
days.krestonPM: Give him his own small bucket with three leaves in it and a job carrying them the length of the yard. At 17 months he will drop the bucket every fourth step. Keep him well away from the bags, at the open end of the yard with something to kick.

insight.headline: A unit only works if it stays the same size, and that's the hard part.
paras: Six is a number Azlyn owns. Six scoops is a measurement, and it holds together only while the scoop refuses to change. That idea sits underneath every ruler, cup and kitchen scale she will ever use, and three-year-olds take their time getting to it, because nothing else in her world holds a fixed size on purpose. Swapping the pot for a mug hands her the failure without a word from you. Piaget built a famous experiment out of the same confusion, with two glasses and a pitcher of water. Yours costs a spilled jar and four minutes.

days.safety: Trash bags are a suffocation risk. Keep them out of Kreston's reach the whole time and put the spare bags away before he comes outside. Wash both children's hands after leaf litter, and check the pile for glass and dog mess before she puts her hands in it. Dried beans, lentils and rice go into a 17-month-old's mouth and nose, so keep Kreston in the high chair or out of the kitchen while the tub is open, and sweep the floor around the table before he walks through it.

days.title: The Countdown Jar
days.prepTonight: Wash the twenty-nine pebbles and leave them to dry on a dish towel, with the two jars, the marker and the crayons beside them.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Tree With Nothing Left On It

opening.title: Twenty-Nine Stones on the Table
opening.need: 29 flat pebbles or wine corks · a clear table.
steps: Pour the pebbles into the middle of the table and let her push them around.
Lay them into rows of ten with her. Two full rows and one row of nine.
Ask how many days she thinks are in the pile. Take her number and tell her the pile has a job at 9:15.

main.title: One Stone Out Every Day
materials: 1 second empty jar, also with a lid
Paper and sticky tape, for the label
steps: Stand the clear jar on the table and let her drop the pebbles in one at a time, counting as she goes. Twenty-nine, and she needs help past twenty.
Tell her what the jar is for. One pebble out every evening after dinner, and the last one on the night she turns four.
She draws the label on the paper: a cake, four candles, whatever she wants. Crayons, her hands, no corrections.
Write DECEMBER 20, AZLYN IS FOUR under her drawing in marker and tape the label round the jar.
Stand the second jar beside it, empty. That one fills as the first one empties, and the last pebble lands in it on her birthday night.
Do the first one now. One pebble out, into the empty jar, lids on, both jars on a high shelf where she can see them and not reach them.
main.tip: Count the filling jar every night and the emptying one every few days. Counting up what has gone is the easy half, and it keeps her in the game.

outside.title: The Tree With Nothing Left On It
paras: Go back to the tree you have walked past all year, the one you looked at on the first day of January. It has nothing on it now. Stand under it and look straight up through the branches. Ask her about the summer. Bring home one fallen twig with buds on it, because next year's buds are already there. The leaves being off was one of the markers you gave her in July for the bottle on the shelf, so tell her the leaves are off now and let her go and look at it.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and he needs to touch this one. Hold him up to the trunk and let him get both palms flat on the bark, then put a twig in each hand. Two-word combinations are starting, so feed him the pair he can copy: big tree, said while he is touching it.

second.title: The Same Tree, Four Times
second.intro: One long strip of paper along the floor, the same tree drawn on it four times, and this morning's twig taped onto it.
materials: 1 long strip of paper: a wallpaper offcut, or 4 sheets taped end to end
The twig from this morning's walk
1 pressed leaf, if you kept one
A summer photo of the tree, or her memory of it
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
steps: Roll the strip out and fold it into four panels. She kneels at one end and works left to right.
Panel one is now: bare branches, nothing on them. The twig sits beside her as the model.
Panel two is spring. Small green dots on the branch ends for the buds she found this morning.
Panel three is summer, and it wants more crayon than the other three together. Show her the photo, then leave her to it.
Panel four is autumn: orange, red, half the leaves on the ground. Tape the pressed leaf onto this panel.
Tape the twig onto panel one. Walk her along the strip from one to four, then take her hand and carry it round from four back to one.

Tape the strip along the wall at her height, low enough for her to touch the panel the house is in today. If you are marking the frame this month, this is the afternoon for it. Two pencil lines on the door frame, name and date beside each, while the strip is still going up.
second.tip: Draw the trunk on all four panels yourself before she starts, in the same place each time. Four different trees on one strip loses the whole idea.

alternatives: Two panels only: today and summer.
Draw the same tree on four paper plates instead of a strip.
Rub the bark with a crayon through paper and tape that on.
outAgain: The duck pond, and see how much of it has gone quiet since October
The riverside path, for how far you can see through the bare trees now
A walk to find the last tree in the neighborhood still holding its leaves
Round the block before the light goes, flashlight in her pocket
days.krestonPM: Tape a spare sheet of paper to the floor at the far end and give him two crayons. At 17 months he scribbles with his whole arm from the shoulder and works off the edge of the paper. Lift him to the wall when the strip goes up and let him press one piece of tape flat.

insight.headline: Counting down is much harder than counting up.
paras: Azlyn's number words came in as a chant, learned in one direction like a song. Going backwards means dropping the chant and working out what comes before, which asks her to hold the whole line of numbers in mind. Most children manage counting up to twenty a year before counting down from ten arrives, and that gap is the standard shape of it rather than a hole in her. A jar that empties gives her the idea in a form she can hold: fewer pebbles tonight than last night, and a smaller number said out loud to match. The counting follows the handful.

days.safety: Twenty-nine loose pebbles and a 17-month-old who walks and pockets things do not mix. Count at the table with Kreston in the high chair, sweep the floor before he is down, and keep both jars on the high shelf between evenings. Never leave the lids off.

days.title: The Year Goes Round
days.prepTonight: Put two paper plates, the crayons, the marker and the stickers on the table, and dig out a log slice from the firewood pile for Wednesday if you have one.

opening.title: Folding the Circle Into Four
steps: Fold the plate in half with her, then in half again, and open it flat. Two creases, four quarters.
Give each quarter a season and a color: winter, spring, summer, autumn, going round in one direction. She colors a stripe of each.
Ask her which quarter today lives in. Send her to the window to look.

main.title: Giving Every Month a Face
materials: 2 paper plates, or 2 circles cut from card
A length of wool, knotted through the middle so the plates turn, or a brass fastener
steps: Split each colored quarter of this morning's plate into three with the marker. Twelve wedges, numbered 1 to 12 going round.
Name each month as you write its number and let her tell you what happens in it. December is presents, July is the paddling pool.
Every wedge gets a face drawn by Azlyn: grumpy January, hot July, whatever she decides. She colors each wedge to match its season stripe.
Stickers on the birthdays: hers on December, Kreston's on June, Brooklyn's on December, Joseph's on September. Say each name as the sticker lands.
Cut one wedge-shaped window out of the second plate. You do the cutting, with her hands off the table.
Push the wool through the middle of both plates and knot it either side so the top plate turns. One month shows at a time, and she can spin the year round.
main.tip: Turn the wheel forward past December and let it come round to January again. The year joining up is why the shape is a circle.

outside.title: Where the Frost Held On
paras: Late November frost hangs on past ten in the places the sun never reaches. Hunt for it there: the north side of a wall, under a parked car, in the shadow of a hedge. Put her hand flat on a frosted car roof and then on a clear one. Come back on the way home and see which ones have given in.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and cold is worth meeting with his hands rather than through the stroller cover. Let him touch frost on a wall for a few seconds, then get the gloves back on. He will pull his hand back and want to do it again. Say cold every time, the same word in the same voice.

second.title: Posting Everybody Into Their Month
second.intro: Twelve pockets go down the back of a door, and everyone in the family gets posted into the month they belong to. The wheel is how she finds them.
materials: Photos, or hand-written name cards, for everyone in the family
A door, or a clear stretch of wall
steps: Number the twelve envelopes 1 to 12, big enough to read across the room. She hands them to you in order.
Tape them down the door in two columns of six, opening upward, low enough for her to reach.
Make the cards together: one per person, per pet, and anyone whose birthday she knows. She picks the photo or scribbles a face, you write the name and month on the front.
Hand her one card. She turns the wheel to find the month written on it, matches the number to an envelope and posts it.
Work through the family, then the pets, then the days she cares about: Christmas, Thanksgiving, the day Kreston was born.
Count the envelopes with something in them and the ones still empty.
Leave the door up. Anything she draws between now and Christmas gets posted into the month it happened in.
second.tip: Put her own card in last and make a fuss of it. December is a busy pocket in this house, and finding out she shares her month with Brooklyn is the sort of fact she repeats for weeks.

alternatives: Four pockets, one per season, and skip the months.
Draw the family instead of using photos.
Post one card a day for twelve days.
Line the envelopes up on the floor and walk along them.
outAgain: Swimming, and warmer than anything outdoors today
Indoor playground, if the pool is booked out before the holidays
The library, a day early
A hot chocolate somewhere with a radiator
The indoor play center
days.krestonPM: He has swimming too. At 17 months he walks the shallow end holding one of your hands and would let go given half a chance, so stay within arm's reach the whole time. Twenty-five minutes is his limit before the cold gets him. Back home, give him three spare envelopes to post into the bottom pocket.

insight.headline: Giving a number a personality is what makes it stick.
paras: Twelve months is an abstraction, and Azlyn has no shelf to put it on. A face, a color and a bad mood for January give her twelve hooks instead of twelve labels. Memory researchers have known for decades that material tied to emotion and imagery gets recalled far better than the same material learned flat, and three-year-olds run on that harder than adults do. She will remember August as the yellow one with the sunburn long after she has forgotten it is number eight. The number comes later and attaches itself to the face she already knows, which is the order most of her learning arrives in.

days.safety: The scissors are adult-only and Kreston is 17 months and fast on his feet. Cut the window while he is in the high chair or out of the room, and the scissors go back on the high shelf the moment it is done. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Steeper and Steeper
days.prepTonight: Clear a run of floor and stand the board against the wall with ten books beside it, and peel enough potatoes for tomorrow's table and leave them in cold water.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Hill She Can Make Steeper

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: A Ring for Every Year She's Had

opening.title: Books Under One End
opening.need: the board · a stack of books · 1 orange.
steps: Lay the board flat on the floor and roll the orange along it. It goes nowhere.
Slide one book under the top end and roll the orange again. She pushes the book under.
Ask her what happens with two books. Take her prediction, do not test it yet, and tell her the whole hill gets built at 9:15.

main.title: The Hill She Can Make Steeper
materials: 1 flat board, an ironing board, or a big flattened box
A stack of 8–10 books, all about the same thickness
1 orange, 1 tennis ball, 1 pine cone, 1 toy car, 1 potato
Chalk, or masking tape, to mark where each one stops
Paper and 1 marker, for the record
steps: One book under the top end of the board. Send all five objects down, one at a time, in the same order every round. Mark where each one stops with chalk or a tape strip and write the name beside it.
Before every run, ask her to call which one goes furthest.
Second book. Same five, same order, fresh marks.
She adds the books from here on. Around five or six the cone and the potato start moving.
Write the record on paper: five rows, one object each, a tick against every height it traveled. She points at the row with the most ticks.
Let her build it as steep as it will stand and send everything down at once.
main.tip: Keep the books the same thickness so each one is a fair step. A steeper slope only reads as a rule if every step up is the same size.

outside.title: Rolling Down the Bank Herself
paras: Find a grass bank, the slope beside the path, or the mound at the edge of the park, and let her roll down it on her side with her arms tucked in. Do it once yourself so she knows you meant it. Then walk her to the flat and ask her to roll there. She has to do all the work herself, and she will tell you so. Wet grass and old clothes.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and a slope is a whole problem for him. Let him walk down a gentle one holding your finger and watch his knees work out the difference. Going up is easy for him; coming down is the skill. On the way home, roll a ball down the bank for him to chase and kick back up.

second.title: A Ring for Every Year She's Had
second.intro: A tree writes its age down one ring at a time, and everyone in the house gets a disc of their own this afternoon. Hers has three rings on it until December 20.
materials: 4 paper plates, or 4 circles cut from card
1 log slice from the firewood pile, or a photo of a cut stump
steps: Put the log slice in her hands and count the rings with her finger on them. Get as far as she has patience for, then tell her the number.
Her plate first. Three rings in crayon, drawn from the middle out, one for each year she has had.
Kreston's next. One ring, and she will think it looks wrong. Let her say so and let it stand.
Yours and Joseph's take too long to draw one at a time, so let her scribble rings until she has had enough and then write the real number in the middle in marker.
Write each name round the edge of its plate with the marker while she says who it belongs to.
Lay the four discs on the floor in order, fewest rings to most. She works out the order.
Go back to the log slice and count the rings once more. That tree was older than everyone on the floor put together.
second.tip: Say the word year the way she meets it: one birthday to the next. Three rings means she has had three birthdays.

alternatives: One disc each, no counting, rings only.
Press crayon over the real log slice through paper for a bark rubbing.
Count the rings on a chopping board or a wooden spoon.
Draw a family of trees, tallest to shortest.
outAgain: The library, every two weeks, and something about trees or winter if they have it
Indoor playground, if the library is packed the day before Thanksgiving
The store, and let her carry one thing for tomorrow
The park on the way home, for one more go on the bank
A café and the new book read cover to cover once
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and put him down in the board-book corner. At 17 months he pulls books off the shelf faster than you can reshelve them. Let Azlyn pick his one and carry it to the desk. Back home, give him a spare plate and a crayon and let him work beside her on the floor.

insight.headline: Steeper is a variable she can control, and that's rare.
paras: Most of the physical world happens to Azlyn at a size she cannot alter. The slope is different, because one book under the end changes it and her hands put the book there. That turns her from an observer into the person running the experiment, and children who control the variable predict better and remember longer than children shown the same demonstration. She is also meeting the shape of an experiment: change one thing, keep the rest the same, watch what moves. The word for that arrives in about ten years. The habit starts on a board and a stack of books.

days.safety: Stack the books against a wall so the pile has something to lean on, and take the board down between rounds instead of leaving it propped. Kreston is 17 months and goes to whatever is moving, so keep him out of the run and keep the pine cone off the floor while he is down there. Check the bank for stones and dog mess before she rolls down it.

days.title: Thanksgiving Dinner and the Long Drive
days.prepTonight: The peeled potatoes are in cold water in the fridge. Set her tray, the masher, the big bowl and the wooden spoon out on a low counter.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: One Dish With Nobody Else's Hands In It

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Car That Goes Wherever She Says

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Carrying Her Dish to the Table

opening.title: Her Ingredients on One Tray
opening.need: 1 tray · the 6 peeled potatoes, from last night · the butter · the milk in a small pitcher · 1 serving dish.
steps: Put the tray in front of her and load it together: butter, the pitcher of milk, the empty serving dish.
Tell her the job. One dish for the table today, made by her, with nobody else's hands in it.
Let her carry the tray to her spot at the counter. It stays there while you boil the potatoes.

main.title: One Dish With Nobody Else's Hands In It
materials: 6 potatoes, peeled last night and boiled by you this morning
A splash of milk, in a pitcher
1 card and 1 marker, for the label
steps: Drain the potatoes and let the steam go off them. Tip them into the large bowl in front of her.
Hand her the masher and take your hands off it. It takes ten minutes and it will have lumps in it.
Butter in, stirred through with the wooden spoon. A warm potato takes it, a cold one does not.
Milk from the pitcher, a splash at a time, with her saying when to stop. Let her overshoot.
Taste it together. Salt if she says salt. She spoons it into the serving dish and smooths the top with the spoon.

Cover the dish and put it in the fridge. It comes out to warm through while the table is laid, and she carries it over at four. She draws on the card, you write MASHED POTATOES, BY AZLYN underneath in marker, and it stands against her dish all through dinner.
main.tip: Take the dish as it comes. Somebody at that table will offer to fix the lumps, and the answer is no.

outside.title: A Thank-You at Every Corner
paras: Walk the block before the kitchen gets hot. At every corner, both of you stop and name one thing you are thankful for, then turn. Give yours a real answer and she will follow. Hers will be the dog, the mashed potatoes and a puddle.

days.infant: Kreston is 17 months and today is loud. Get him outside for the whole forty-five minutes before the house fills up, and let him walk as much of it as he wants. On the corners, say your thank-you to him at his eye level. Two-word combinations are starting, so use the ones that fit: big dinner, hot oven.

second.title: The Car That Goes Wherever She Says
second.intro: The kitchen is busy and the house is filling up, so she gets the far corner of the living room and a car that goes anywhere she names.
materials: 1 cardboard circle for the steering wheel
1 bag with a snack and a drink in it
steps: Line the chairs up two by two and put the cushions on the seats. She decides who drives.
Tape the cardboard circle to the back of the front chair. That is the wheel.
Ask where you are going. Take her first answer and hold her to it. She draws the place on the paper plate and tapes it where a windshield would be.
She draws the route on the paper: home at one end, the place at the other, three things you pass. Those are the stops.
Load the bag, put it in the back, big light off and flashlight on. Drive, and she makes the engine noise.
Stop at each of her three things. Get out, do the thing, get back in. Ask where you are heading each time you set off.
Arrive. Everybody gets out. You swap seats, she picks somewhere new, and the second journey gets three stops of its own.
second.tip: Keep asking where you are going, at every stop, all the way through. Holding a destination across three interruptions is the hardest thing she does today.

alternatives: Two chairs, one steering wheel, no map.
Build a bus and give everyone a paper ticket.
Pack the bag and drive nowhere, eating the snack in the car.
outAgain: The bakery, if anything is open, and the long way round if it is not
A walk round the block with whoever needs to get out of the kitchen
Deliver a plate of something to a neighbor and take the long way back
The green space with a ball, for anyone who has eaten too much
days.krestonPM: Put him in the back seat with a cushion and the bag. At 17 months he takes the snack out, hands it to you, and wants it put back, and he can run that game for ten minutes at a time, coming back to it twice. Once the house gets loud, the car is a good place for the two of them to be.

insight.headline: Driving somewhere imaginary requires her to hold a destination in mind.
paras: A cardboard steering wheel looks like nothing, and the work behind it is considerable. Azlyn has to keep a place she cannot see fixed in her head while her body sits in a chair, then hold that idea through three interruptions and get back to it. Psychologists call this working memory with a goal attached, and it is the machinery she will use to follow a two-step instruction, finish a drawing she started yesterday or read a sentence to its end. Pretend play loads it harder than most tasks you could set her, and she volunteers for it without being asked twice.

days.safety: The oven is on all day and Kreston is 17 months, walking, climbing and pulling at handles. Keep him out of the kitchen while trays move, turn every pan handle inward, and never set a hot dish down on the table edge. Her mashing happens well away from the stovetop. Guests bring food down to coffee-table height, so whole nuts, hard candy, whole grapes, olives and popcorn stay up on the counter. Tell every guest that rule before they sit down. Kreston's plate gets grapes quartered lengthways and everything else cut smaller than his fingernail. Sweep the floor between the meal and letting him back down on it.
